channel.title: Jiva blog: building Jiva in the open
channel.description: One product manager, no code, building a fully-local Mac meeting assistant with AI, documented as it happens.

item.title: Certify before you optimise
item.description: I spent weeks tuning the speaker engine without a reliable way to measure it. Then I built the boring thing — an eval set — and found the engine was already strong.

item.title: The same person, months later
item.description: The feature I'm proudest of demos the worst, because it only means anything over time: recognising the same voice across separate meetings, weeks or months apart, on the device.

item.title: Not everything said in a meeting is a decision
item.description: “Maybe we should raise the price” and “we’re raising the price” read the same in a transcript. Jiva marks the difference by tagging each line as said, decided, or an action.

item.title: Repairing mangled names — and the fix that broke everything
item.description: Speech recognition garbles names and figures. My first attempt to auto-repair them “fixed” Whichever into Whisper.

item.title: Why I made the app refuse to guess a name
item.description: Jiva knows there are two people on a call long before it knows their names. Putting a real name on a voice too early is how you poison the record.

item.title: Confidently wrong: when silence is worse than an error
item.description: A denied permission didn't throw an error. It returned silence — so the app confidently attributed a whole meeting to one person.

item.title: One person became four
item.description: A two-person call that showed up as four speakers, and what fixing it taught me about not trusting the machine's confidence.

item.title: “Me is not me”: the bug that taught me attribution is an audio problem
item.description: I thought transcription would be the hard part. The hard part is knowing who said what — and it starts much lower down, in the audio.

item.title: One build constraint quietly shaped the whole app
item.description: I wanted everything in one native language. A limitation in how Apple's ML framework builds meant the AI part had to stay Python — so I designed around it.

item.title: Leaving Python for Swift, and deleting the thing that worked
item.description: The first working Jiva was Python. I threw most of it away and rebuilt the core natively. As a non-engineer, deleting the thing that already ran felt wrong. It was right.

item.title: A test that cannot fail is not a test
item.description: As Jiva grew I got scared of silently breaking old things. So I built a regression net — and then made myself prove it could actually catch a mistake.

item.title: How a non-coder debugs: read, don’t reproduce
item.description: I've never reproduced some of Jiva's hardest bugs. I found them by reading the code against the exact symptom until the failure became inevitable on paper.

item.title: 143 decisions in three months
item.description: What a dated decision log does that your memory can't — and why it's the least glamorous and most important artifact in the whole project.

item.title: What building with AI actually breaks on
item.description: Everyone asks whether the AI can write the code. The answer is mostly yes. The real breakage is remembering why — and vouching for what came back.

item.title: The markdown “brain” that let a non-coder ship
item.description: The reason I could build this isn't the model. It's a plain set of markdown files that give any AI session full memory of the project.

item.title: A product manager decides to build systems software
item.description: I can't write code. I'm building native Mac audio software anyway, entirely with AI. Here is why that is less reckless than it sounds — and where it might still break.

item.title: I killed my last startup, and it made me surer about this one
item.description: Before Jiva I spent months on Cryptowave. Walking away from it left me with three rules I now use to decide what to build.

item.title: The biggest lever in AI work is context, not a cleverer prompt
item.description: Most advice about getting more out of AI is about the prompt. In my experience the far bigger lever is the source material you give it.

item.title: The Granola-and-Claude moment that started Jiva
item.description: How using a meeting recorder and an AI together — and then hitting the same wall three times — turned into Jiva, a fully-local second brain for the Mac.
